WRONGFUL TERMINATION IN VIOLATION OF PUBLIC POLICY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Morgan T. Ellis · Acme Manufacturing, Inc.

INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND — ALLEGED PUBLIC-POLICY TERMINATION
I, Morgan T. Ellis, am completing this information sheet in connection with the ending of my employment with Acme Manufacturing, Inc., which this document treats as having ended on March 14, 2026. The activity or report I believe may be legally protected is described here as: Reported suspected wage-and-hour violations to the payroll manager. The law, regulation, or public policy I believe may have been implicated is described here as: California wage-and-hour law requiring payment of overtime. This information sheet provides background for someone evaluating whether a termination may have violated public policy under California law. It is not a court filing, a demand letter, an employer policy, or a legal determination of any kind, and completing it does not establish, prove, or determine that Morgan T. Ellis's termination by Acme Manufacturing, Inc. violated any public policy, statute, or law, or that any claim described in this document is valid. Only a court, or another body with legal authority to decide the question, can determine whether a specific termination was unlawful.

CALIFORNIA'S AT-WILL DEFAULT — AND ITS STATUTORY LIMITS
California law presumes that employment with no specified term may be ended by either the employer or the employee at will, for any reason or no reason, on notice to the other. That default is not absolute: California has enacted specific statutes making it unlawful for an employer to end someone's employment, or take other adverse action against them, for defined reasons — including some of the reasons described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employment, having no specified term, may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other. Employment for a specified term means an employment for a period greater than one month."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2922 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2922.)
  Known gap: This is California's own general at-will statute, used here as real evidence of the default rule against which the statutory exceptions described in this document operate — not a claim about which state's law actually governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any specific termination was, or was not, lawful. Beyond this statutory default, California courts have long recognized a separate, judicially created exception to at-will employment for termination that violates a fundamental public policy — commonly discussed under the case name Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co., 27 Cal.3d 167 (1980) — along with a multi-part test courts use to decide whether a particular policy is sufficiently "fundamental" to support that kind of claim, commonly discussed under cases including Gantt v. Sentry Insurance, 1 Cal.4th 1083 (1992), and Stevenson v. Superior Court, 16 Cal.4th 880 (1997). This research session's CourtListener case-law lookups returned a daily-rate-limit error on every attempt (across its search, endpoint, and item-lookup tools), and a direct fetch to courtlistener.com was separately blocked by this environment's network egress controls; as a result, this document does not state the holding of Tameny, the exact formulation of the fundamental-policy test, or any other case-law point as verified fact, and cites no case law for any of it. That is disclosed here as an honest gap rather than filled with an unverified citation. This clause cites a single statutory section (Labor Code § 2922); no additional independent source was sought for the at-will default itself. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any specific termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

STATUTORY PROTECTION FOR REPORTING A SUSPECTED LEGAL VIOLATION
California law prohibits an employer from making, adopting, or enforcing any rule, regulation, or policy that would prevent an employee from disclosing information to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee, or to another employee with authority to investigate, discover, or correct a violation, where the employee has reasonable cause to believe the information discloses a violation of a state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation. Separately, the same statute prohibits an employer from retaliating against an employee for making that kind of disclosure, or because the employer believes the employee disclosed or may disclose that kind of information. This protection applies regardless of whether making the disclosure is part of the employee's own job duties.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not make, adopt, or enforce any rule, regulation, or policy preventing an employee from disclosing information to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee, or to another employee who has authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance, or from providing information to, or testifying before, any public body conducting an investigation, hearing, or inquiry, if the employee has reasonable cause to believe that the information discloses a violation of state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation, regardless of whether disclosing the information is part of the employee’s job duties."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  "An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee for disclosing information, or because the employer believes that the employee disclosed or may disclose information, to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee or another employee who has the authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance, or for providing information to, or testifying before, any public body conducting an investigation, hearing, or inquiry, if the employee has reasonable cause to believe that the information discloses a violation of state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation, regardless of whether disclosing the information is part of the employee’s job duties."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  Known gap: Both citations in this clause are to different subsections of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(a) and § 1102.5(b), as amended effective January 1, 2024 — which is disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as two independent sources. This is California's own statute, used as real evidence of a specific, currently operative statutory anti-retaliation protection — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any particular disclosure actually qualifies for this protection or that any particular termination was retaliatory. Whether an employee in fact had "reasonable cause to believe" the disclosed information showed a legal violation, and whether the disclosure was actually made to one of the specific recipients this statute covers, are fact-specific questions this document does not resolve. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

REFUSING TO BREAK THE LAW, PROTECTION CARRIED FROM A PRIOR JOB, AND GOVERNMENT-EMPLOYEE REPORTS
The same statute also prohibits an employer from retaliating against an employee for refusing to participate in an activity that would violate a state or federal statute, or that would violate or fail to comply with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation. It separately prohibits retaliation against an employee for having exercised these same protections in a former job, not only the current one. And it specifically treats a report made by a government employee to their own employer as a covered disclosure under this statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee for refusing to participate in an activity that would result in a violation of state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  "An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee for having exercised their rights under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) in any former employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  "A report made by an employee of a government agency to their employer is a disclosure of information to a government or law enforcement agency pursuant to subdivisions (a) and (b)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  Known gap: All three citations in this clause are to different subsections of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(c), (d), and (e) — which is disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. This is California's own statute, used as real evidence of the scope of this specific statutory protection — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any particular refusal, prior-job activity, or report actually falls within this statute's coverage in a specific case. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

CIVIL PENALTY AND ATTORNEY'S FEES UNDER THIS STATUTE
In addition to any other available remedy, California law makes an employer who violates this statute liable for a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per employee for each violation, awarded to the employee who was retaliated against. In assessing the amount of that penalty, the Labor Commissioner considers the nature and seriousness of the violation, including the type of violation, the economic or mental harm suffered, and the chilling effect on the exercise of employment rights in the workplace. Separately, a court may award reasonable attorney's fees to a plaintiff who brings a successful lawsuit for a violation of this statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In addition to other remedies available, an employer is liable for a civil penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000) per employee for each violation of this section to be awarded to the employee who was retaliated against."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  "In assessing this penalty, the Labor Commissioner shall consider the nature and seriousness of the violation based on the evidence obtained during the course of the investigation. The Labor Commissioner’s consideration of the nature and seriousness of the violation shall include, but is not limited to, the type of violation, the economic or mental harm suffered, and the chilling effect on the exercise of employment rights in the workplace, and shall be considered to the extent evidence obtained during the investigation concerned any of these or other relevant factors."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(f)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  "The court is authorized to award reasonable attorney’s fees to a plaintiff who brings a successful action for a violation of these provisions."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(j) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  Known gap: All three citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(f)(1), (f)(2), and (j) — which is disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. This is California's own statute, used as real evidence of the specific civil-penalty and fee-shifting structure this particular statute carries — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any specific violation occurred or that any specific penalty or fee award would result. The $10,000 figure is a per-employee, per-violation cap the Labor Commissioner may assess after considering the listed factors; it is not an amount awarded automatically or in every case. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

A SEPARATE STATUTE PROTECTING WAGE CLAIMS AND LABOR COMMISSIONER COMPLAINTS
A different California statute separately prohibits an employer from discharging an employee, or otherwise discriminating or retaliating against them, because the employee filed a bona fide complaint or claim relating to rights under the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction, made a written or oral complaint that they are owed unpaid wages, or exercised certain other rights this statute covers. An employee retaliated against for one of these reasons is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits, and if the employer's adverse action happens within 90 days of the protected activity, the law creates a rebuttable presumption in the employee's favor. This statute also carries its own civil penalty of up to $10,000 per employee for each violation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A person shall not discharge an employee or in any manner discriminate, retaliate, or take any adverse action against any employee or applicant for employment because the employee or applicant engaged in any conduct delineated in this chapter, including the conduct described in subdivision (k) of Section 96, and Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 1101) of Part 3 of Division 2, or because the employee or applicant for employment has filed a bona fide complaint or claim or instituted or caused to be instituted any proceeding under or relating to their rights that are under the jurisdiction of the Labor Commissioner, made a written or oral complaint that they are owed unpaid wages, or because the employee has initiated any action or notice pursuant to Section 2699, or has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding pursuant to that section, or because of the exercise by the employee or applicant for employment on behalf of themselves or others of any rights afforded them."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.6(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.6.)
  "Any employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, retaliated against, subjected to an adverse action, or in any other manner discriminated against in the terms and conditions of their employment because the employee engaged in any conduct delineated in this chapter, including the conduct described in subdivision (k) of Section 96, and Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 1101) of Part 3 of Division 2, or because the employee has made a bona fide complaint or claim to the division pursuant to this part, or because the employee has initiated any action or notice pursuant to Section 2699 shall be entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by those acts of the employer. If an employer engages in any action prohibited by this section within 90 days of the protected activity specified in this section, there shall be a rebuttable presumption in favor of the employee’s claim."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.6(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.6.)
  "In addition to other remedies available, an employer who violates this section is liable for a civil penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000) per employee for each violation of this section, to be awarded to the employee or employees who suffered the violation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.6(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.6.)
  Known gap: The citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 98.6(a), (b)(1), and (b)(3) — which is disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. This is California's own statute, used as real evidence of a second, separate statutory anti-retaliation protection distinct from Labor Code § 1102.5 addressed elsewhere in this document — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any particular complaint or activity actually falls within this statute's coverage, or that any specific employer action was retaliatory. The 90-day presumption described here is rebuttable, not conclusive — an employer can offer a non-retaliatory explanation for its action within that window. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

A SEPARATE STATUTE: TERMINATION BASED ON OFF-DUTY CANNABIS USE OR METABOLITE TESTING
Since January 1, 2024, a separate California statute — part of the Fair Employment and Housing Act — independently makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against a person in termination, or any other term or condition of employment, based on "the person's use of cannabis off the job and away from the workplace," or based on "an employer-required drug screening test that has found the person to have nonpsychoactive cannabis metabolites in their hair, blood, urine, or other bodily fluids." The metabolite point exists because standard urine and hair tests detect nonpsychoactive metabolites that can remain in the body for days or weeks after use, long after any impairment has ended, so a positive result on that kind of test doesn't by itself show current impairment. This is a distinct statutory protection from the disclosure- and wage-retaliation statutes described elsewhere in this document: it turns on the stated reason for the termination itself, not on whether the employee made a report or complaint.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "it is unlawful for an employer to discriminate against a person in hiring, termination, or any term or condition of employment, or otherwise penalizing a person, if the discrimination is based upon any of the following: (A) The person’s use of cannabis off the job and away from the workplace."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(a)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Employment and Housing Act, off-duty cannabis use protection applied to termination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  "An employer-required drug screening test that has found the person to have nonpsychoactive cannabis metabolites in their hair, blood, urine, or other bodily fluids."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(a)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, nonpsychoactive-metabolite screening protection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  Known gap: The introductory language of subdivision (a)(1) and paragraph (A) within it are part of the same sentence of the same statutory subdivision, Government Code § 12954(a)(1); the metabolite-testing point in paragraph (B) is a separate paragraph of that same subdivision. All are being treated together as one connected source, not as independent corroborating sources. This same statutory section, including its exemptions, is independently described in more detail in this corpus's separate Hiring-category document, the Pre-Employment and Workplace Drug Testing Information Sheet — this clause does not repeat that document's full citation set, and the next clause in this document covers only the exemptions most relevant to a termination that has already occurred. This document does not describe the Civil Rights Department's administrative complaint and right-to-sue process that generally applies to a claim brought directly under this statute, as distinct from the direct-to-court statutes described elsewhere in this document; that procedural framework was not independently verified in this research session and is not addressed here. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific termination was, or was not, based on off-duty cannabis use or a metabolite test result. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

LIMITS AND EXCEPTIONS TO THAT PROTECTION
That protection has specific limits relevant to evaluating a termination. It does not apply at all to an employee in the building and construction trades. It does not give an employee the right to possess, be impaired by, or use cannabis on the job, and it does not affect an employer's rights or obligations to maintain a drug- and alcohol-free workplace. It does not preempt any state or federal law requiring applicants or employees to be tested for controlled substances — including as a condition of federal funding, federal licensing-related benefits, or a federal contract. And it does not apply at all to positions that require a federal government background investigation or security clearance under U.S. Department of Defense regulations, or equivalent regulations of other federal agencies.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This subdivision does not apply to an employee in the building and construction trades."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, building and construction trades carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  "This section does not permit an employee to possess, to be impaired by, or to use, cannabis on the job, or affect the rights or obligations of an employer to maintain a drug- and alcohol-free workplace, as specified in Section 11362.45 of the Health and Safety Code, or any other rights or obligations of an employer specified by state or federal law or regulation."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, on-the-job use and drug-free workplace carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  "This section does not preempt state or federal laws requiring applicants or employees to be tested for controlled substances, including laws and regulations requiring applicants or employees to be tested, or the manner in which they are tested, as a condition of employment, receiving federal funding or federal licensing-related benefits, or entering into a federal contract."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, no preemption of federal or state testing requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  "This section does not apply to applicants or employees hired for positions that require a federal government background investigation or security clearance in accordance with regulations issued by the United States Department of Defense pursuant to Part 117 of Title 32 of the Code of Federal Regulations, or equivalent regulations applicable to other agencies."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, federal security-clearance positions excluded (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  Known gap: All four citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section as the previous clause, Government Code § 12954 — subdivisions (a)(2), (d), (e), and (f) — treated together here as one connected source, not as independent corroborating sources. The same exemptions are independently described in this corpus's separate Hiring-category document, the Pre-Employment and Workplace Drug Testing Information Sheet; this clause restates them only because they bear directly on whether a termination falls within the protection described in the previous clause, not as an independent verification effort. Cannabis remains a Schedule I controlled substance under the federal Controlled Substances Act, so a federal contractor or a federally regulated position can still require testing for it regardless of this state law, exactly as this clause states. This clause does not determine whether any particular employee, position, or employer falls within one of these exemptions, and it does not determine that any specific termination was, or was not, lawful. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

A DIFFERENT KIND OF FILING DEADLINE — AND WHAT WASN'T VERIFIED HERE
Separately from the wage-claim and civil-penalty statutes described elsewhere in this document, California law sets a two-year filing deadline for an action for injury to, or the death of, an individual caused by the wrongful act or neglect of another — the general statute of limitations that applies to an ordinary personal-injury tort claim. This is a different kind of deadline, tied to a different kind of claim, than the wage-claim deadlines and statutory penalty provisions addressed elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Within two years: An action for assault, battery, or injury to, or for the death of, an individual caused by the wrongful act or neglect of another."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 335.1 (California Legislative Information text), California Code of Civil Procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=335.1.)
  Known gap: This is California's own general personal-injury tort statute of limitations, used here as real evidence of how California law structures an ordinary tort claim's filing deadline — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any specific termination was wrongful. Two related points this clause does not establish, and could not verify in this research session: first, whether a common-law wrongful-termination-in-violation-of-public-policy claim — the kind of claim this document is named for, commonly discussed under the case name Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co., 27 Cal.3d 167 (1980) — is treated by California courts as the kind of personal-injury tort this two-year deadline covers, as opposed to some other claim classification with a different deadline; second, whether such a claim is treated as carrying tort remedies (potentially including emotional-distress and punitive damages) as distinct from the narrower remedies available on a straightforward unpaid-wage claim. Both are case-law questions. CourtListener, the case-law research tool used throughout this research session, returned a daily-rate-limit error ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") on every attempt made during this session — across its search tool, its call_endpoint tool (tried against the clusters and courts endpoints), and its get_endpoint_item tool — and a direct fetch to courtlistener.com was separately blocked by this environment's network egress controls. As a result, no case law confirming either point was independently verified, and none is cited here; that is disclosed honestly as a gap rather than filled in with an unverified citation or an assumed holding. This clause cites a single statutory section (Code of Civil Procedure § 335.1); no additional independent source was sought for the general tort deadline itself. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy, that any wrongful-termination claim exists, or that any specific remedy would be available in this or any specific case.

expectedJSON.body: Since January 1, 2024, a separate California statute — part of the Fair Employment and Housing Act — independently makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against a person in termination, or any other term or condition of employment, based on "the person's use of cannabis off the job and away from the workplace," or based on "an employer-required drug screening test that has found the person to have nonpsychoactive cannabis metabolites in their hair, blood, urine, or other bodily fluids." The metabolite point exists because standard urine and hair tests detect nonpsychoactive metabolites that can remain in the body for days or weeks after use, long after any impairment has ended, so a positive result on that kind of test doesn't by itself show current impairment. This is a distinct statutory protection from the disclosure- and wage-retaliation statutes described elsewhere in this document: it turns on the stated reason for the termination itself, not on whether the employee made a report or complaint.
